subject: general
question: Why are supervisors often slow to act when banks have problems?

options.text: They do not have the legal power to stop a financial crash.
They prefer to avoid conflict instead of fixing risks early.
They are confused because modern bank rules are too simple.
They use a secret strategy to keep their contracts private.

solution:
The correct answer is '**Option 2**'.

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• ***Hesitation in Oversight:***

 
 
• The passage explicitly notes that in many instances, "supervisors are hesitant to come into conflict with bank management" when weaknesses are first identified.
 
 
 
• ***Preference for Inaction:***
 
 
• The author observes that supervisors often prefer "doing nothing rather than taking corrective action" at the early stages of a problem.
 
 
 
• ***Timing of the Crisis:***
 
 
• This delay occurs exactly when "key issues are building into a problem," suggesting that the failure to act is a result of a desire to avoid immediate friction, even if it leads to long-term instability.
 
 

Therefore, the correct answer is **They prefer to avoid conflict instead of fixing risks early.**

 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Option 1**: Incorrect. The passage discusses "deficiencies in supervisory oversight," implying they have the role and power but fail to execute it effectively.
 
• **Option 3**: Incorrect. The author actually argues that regulation requirements are too complex, not too simple.
 
• **Option 4**: Incorrect. While the author recommends "increased transparency in supervisory contracts," there is no mention of supervisors using a "secret strategy" to keep them private.
